chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
title: Tatum's last years in Los Angeles
summary: Collins saw Tatum, weakened by illness, almost daily; Norman Granz recorded him, and Tatum showed Collins his new house in View Park.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: day and I would have dinner with him at Mike [Limens.] And I felt so sorry because he was just a shell of his former self. He would come up to my hotel room and just sit and I can remember Ben Webster, Harry Edison Addison, Dan Grissom Grisom, we would all lie and do everything, just stand on our heads just to make him laugh. And he -- because he had a hell of a sense of humor. But at this point we really couldn't get to him. I didn't --
Was he still playing then when --

I don't believe -- the only thing he was doing then, Norman Granz Grands was astute shall I say, he was hip enough to realize that he wasn't going to live, I guess, so he had him to come into the studio and do quite a bit of recording during that time. And I was out of town when he died. But --
That recording was the solo piano pieces.

That's right. Norman recorded him right at that time. But he was very ill, you know. But when he bought his first home here in View Park, which was quite a thing -- I don't think there were any blacks at all. He came by and got me up and took me up here to see his new home, and I always believed that Paul [Gadden] bought that home after Art sold it you know -- when he died I think his wife just sold it and I think she sold it to Paul. Paul Gidden.
